unitSummary: The scout, requirements and conceptualizer skills are a reasonable outline of a METHONTOLOGY/NeOn pipeline: CQ elicitation, reuse search, then conceptual modelling behind the auditor's ratification gate. As written they are biomedical/OBO- and BFO-centred and contain several concrete errors. Commands fail as written: `runoak -l`, `-i obo:`, a bare `uv run runoak`, `robot validate`, MIREOT with `--term-file`. `robot verify` is used backwards. Two shared SPARQL queries are broken, there are BFO/RO fact errors, and the stage-authority matrix contradicts the conceptualizer's own job. For inventory-import, the `_shared` references dangle, and the BFO mandate, owl:imports, inverse properties and sameAs/HasKey, and the hand-written YAML/OWL outputs all conflict with the six decisions. The trigger words "import", "model" and "requirements" will also fire on ordinary app work.
keepAsIs: Requirements' use-case to CQ to term to test traceability chain, and its rule that the pre-glossary category column is a lexical guess with no authority (requirements lines 163-187, 240-244)
The conceptualizer's INPUT RULE and edge rule: work only from ratified proposals, and treat an unratified parent or a subClassOf edge as a new candidate for the auditor (lines 43-47, 64-80)

The domain/range decision procedure: SHACL to constrain, broad OWL domain/range only to infer, local restrictions per class. It matches decision 5 (SHACL over stored rows) and anti-pattern #10's NurseJane example
Carrying the unresolved and deferred dispositions index forward through every handoff (conceptualizer lines 244-261)
foundational-analysis.md's failure-mode table (enum-is-taxonomy, identifier-is-identity, vacuous green, parse-only certification), which fits the TS-schema-to-vocabulary work directly
The scout's import-management pitfalls (pin versions, check transitive imports, stale term files) and 'keep non-reused candidates as benchmarks'
MoSCoW prioritization with recorded Won't-Have reasons, and the 'prioritization bias' warning

findings.claim: Every skill opens with "Read these files from `_shared/` before beginning work". In inventory-import those files are not there, so the BFO procedure, the axiom and anti-pattern catalogues and the stage-authority matrix that the conceptualizer's edge rule (line 79) leans on are all unreachable.
findings.evidence: `ls inventory-import/.agents/skills` lists the nine ontology folders but no `_shared`. The beep-effect copy has `_shared/{methodology-backbone.md, bfo-categories.md, axiom-patterns.md, anti-patterns.md, naming-conventions.md, namespaces.json, stage-authority-matrix.yaml, ...}`.
findings.fix: Bring `_shared` over with the skills, adapted as the findings below describe: a gist category guide in place of bfo-categories.md, and namespaces.json gaining a gist prefix. Or inline the few rules each skill actually needs. Then make `bun run docs:check` or a small link check fail on any dangling `_shared/` path.

verification.checked: ls of inventory-import/.agents/skills shows no _shared. diff -rq shows the three skill folders are byte-identical to beep-effect. grep counts the _shared/ references in the copies: scout 5, requirements 4, conceptualizer 12, and every other ontology skill and sparql-expert also has some. beep-effect has the folder at .agents/skills/_shared (anti-patterns, axiom-patterns, bfo-categories, foundational-analysis, methodology-backbone, namespaces.json, naming-conventions, ontoclean-rules.yaml, quality-checklist, schemas/, stage-authority-matrix.yaml, tool-decision-tree) and also a copy at .claude/skills/_shared. Conceptualizer line 79 does cite the matrix.

findings.claim: The conceptualizer requires BFO. Its description says "Aligns to BFO upper ontology", Step 3 runs "the BFO decision procedure", the checklist requires "Every class is aligned to a BFO category", and "Ignoring BFO" is listed as an anti-pattern. Upstream this also contradicts the skill's own reference, bfo-categories.md:196, which says to "Consider DOLCE or no upper ontology" for social and legal domains, which is what an ERP is.
findings.evidence: inventory-import explorations/erp-ontology/DECISIONS.md #4: "a small gist projection, with IOF and ISA-95 as alignments only". bfo-categories.md:195-196 gives software, money, legal entities and prices "no BFO consensus".
findings.fix: Upstream: make the upper ontology a project input recorded in scope.md. The step becomes "align each top class to the project's chosen upper ontology", BFO is one option, and the output is renamed `upper-alignment.md`. Adapt: replace Step 3 with "subClassOf one gist class from the projection list; IOF/ISA-95 only as skos:closeMatch/broadMatch alignment rows in the vocabulary module", and drop the BFO Category column from the glossary.

verification.checked: Every cited line says what the reviewer claims. Conceptualizer line 5 says "Aligns to BFO upper ontology", lines 111-120 give the BFO decision procedure and bfo-alignment.md, line 265 says "Every class is aligned to a BFO category", and lines 274-276 list "Ignoring BFO" as an anti-pattern. bfo-categories.md:196 says "Consider DOLCE or no upper ontology" for legal entities, money and prices. inventory-import DECISIONS.md #4 chose a small gist projection, with IOF and ISA-95 as alignments only.

findings.claim: The skills write term facts into hand-kept files: glossary.csv (labels, definitions), property-design.yaml (domain, range, cardinality, inverse), conceptual-model.yaml (hierarchy), and imports/*.owl. Backbone Phase 4 then has the architect hand-produce ".ttl" and SHACL. Each of these is a second hand-written home for facts that decision 2 gives to one TypeScript vocabulary module, with OWL, SKOS and SHACL generated.
findings.evidence: DECISIONS.md #2: "one TypeScript vocabulary module that owns every term fact ... all Turtle generated". research/02 verdict: "no fact with two homes". Cardinality, datatype and sh:in belong to the record schema.
findings.fix: Adapt: the conceptualizer's output is a proposed diff to `Terms.vocab.ts` (classes, subClassOf, disjointWith, kind/role tag, domain/range, alignments) plus a review note in the packet. Cardinality and datatype come from the record schemas, not property-design.yaml. Paths move from `ontologies/{name}/docs/` into the exploration packet as OKF files with frontmatter. The architect step becomes 'run the generator', not 'write .ttl'.

verification.checked: The conceptualizer outputs glossary.csv, conceptual-model.yaml, bfo-alignment.md, property-design.yaml and axiom-plan.yaml (lines 227-237). Requirements writes .sparql files and CSVs under ontologies/{name}/. methodology-backbone.md:101-102 says the architect "produces: ontology files (.ttl), SHACL shapes". DECISIONS #2 gives every term fact to one TypeScript module with all Turtle generated, and research/02 line 97 puts cardinality, datatype and sh:in in the record schema.

findings.claim: The matrix lists `conceptual-model` as produced by a "generator over ratified proposals" with `llm_allowed: false  # no semantic invention`. It forbids autonomously "assert subsumption, equivalence, disjointness" and "set OWL domain/range, cardinality, functionality, keys". The conceptualizer is an LLM skill that designs property domain, range, cardinality and characteristics (Step 4), selects disjointness and equivalence axioms (Step 5), and is told "Don't leave domain/range as 'to be determined.' Specify even if provisional".
findings.evidence: stage-authority-matrix.yaml lines 47-51, 82-83, read against conceptualizer Steps 4-5 and Anti-Patterns line 279.
findings.fix: Upstream: say that the conceptualizer drafts. Property and axiom-plan entries are proposals with status `proposed` that route through the auditor or the steward for ratification. Set conceptual-model to `llm_allowed: draft-only`, or split it into 'derived model (generator)' and 'design proposals (LLM)'. Replace 'specify even if provisional' with 'propose, and mark it unratified'.

verification.checked: stage-authority-matrix.yaml:47-51 says conceptual-model is made by a "generator over ratified proposals" with llm_allowed: false. Lines 82-83 forbid autonomously asserting subsumption, equivalence or disjointness, and setting domain/range, cardinality, functionality or keys. The conceptualizer designs these in Steps 4-5 and says "Specify even if provisional" at line 280. The matrix is inconsistent with itself as well: lines 32-36 name a "conceptualization agent" as the producer of term-proposals.

findings.claim: `robot verify --input candidate.owl --queries ontologies/{name}/tests/candidate-probes/` is used to test whether a candidate can answer CQ probes. verify treats any result row as a violation and exits with an error, so a candidate that answers a probe 'fails', and one that answers nothing 'passes'. The command is also given a directory, and verify is documented only with query files.
findings.evidence: robot.obolibrary.org/verify: "If the query produces any results, verify will exit with an error message". The documented form is `--queries query-file-1 query-file-2`.
findings.fix: Use `robot query --input candidate.owl --query probe.rq probe.tsv` for each probe and record full, partial or none from the rows. Keep `verify` only for violation queries, which are expected to return zero rows.

verification.checked: ROBOT docs/verify.md: "If the query produces any results, verify will exit with an error message". The documented form is `--queries query-file-1 query-file-2 ... --output-dir some-directory`. Scout line 220 passes a directory to --queries and gives no --output-dir.
verification.correctedFix: Run each probe with `robot query --input candidate.owl --query probe.rq probe.tsv` and record full, partial or none from the rows it returns. Keep `robot verify --queries v1.rq v2.rq --output-dir results/` for violation queries only.

findings.claim: "Syntactic correctness | Required | `robot validate --input candidate.owl`" and the checklist item "Extracted modules load without errors (`robot validate`)". ROBOT documents no `validate` syntax check. Its command list has `validate-profile`, which checks against an OWL 2 profile.
findings.evidence: The robot.obolibrary.org command list has validate-profile and no validate, and /validate returns 404.
findings.fix: Use `robot validate-profile --profile DL --input candidate.owl --output dl-violations.txt` for profile conformance. A parse failure already shows on `robot convert --input candidate.owl --output /dev/null` or on any command that loads the file.

verification.checked: The command registry in ROBOT's CommandLineInterface.java (master) has validate-profile and verify but no validate. https://robot.obolibrary.org/validate returns 404 and /validate-profile returns 200. Scout lines 85, 208 and 245 use `robot validate`.

findings.claim: Three runoak commands fail as written. (a) `runoak -i ols: search "musical instrument" -l 20` fails with "No such option '-l'": search has no limit flag, and top-level `-l` is --preferred-language. (b) `runoak -i obo: ontologies` raises KeyError "Invalid OntologyInterface name: obo". (c) Bare `uv run runoak ...` fails with "Failed to spawn: runoak" in a repository with no pyproject, which describes both repositories, since runoak is not on PATH.
findings.evidence: Run on this machine with `uv run --no-project --with oaklib runoak ...`. The valid adapter list includes `ols`, `bioportal`, `ubergraph`, `lov`, `sqlite` and `obolibrary`, not `obo`.
findings.fix: Use `uv run --no-project --with oaklib runoak -i ols: search "TERM"` and pipe through `head -20` to limit. Replace `-i obo: ontologies` with `-i ubergraph: ontologies`, or with the OBO registry lookup via `-i obolibrary:`. Write the `--with oaklib` form in every snippet.

verification.checked: I checked oaklib main's cli.py. The search command (line 711) has only the terms argument plus the output-type, autolabel and output options, so it has no limit flag. `-l` exists only as the top-level --preferred-language option (line 541). The implementation resolver lists obolibrary, prontolib, simpleobo, sqlite, rdflib, ubergraph, lov and others, with no `obo` scheme. Neither repository has a pyproject.toml, and runoak and robot are not on PATH. I did not re-run the failing commands, because the task forbids installing anything.

findings.claim: `robot extract --method MIREOT --input-iri ... --term-file imports/go_terms.txt` is wrong because MIREOT takes `--lower-term(s)`, `--upper-term(s)` or `--branch-from-term(s)`, not `--term-file`. The trade-off table is also wrong. It calls STAR "All axioms involving the term ... most complete", but STAR is the smallest SLME module. It calls BOT a "good middle ground" that "may include more than needed", which is accurate, but it ranks STAR above BOT for completeness.
findings.evidence: robot.obolibrary.org/extract: MIREOT options are --upper-term(s), --lower-term(s) and --branch-from-term(s). STAR modules are "typically very small" and BOT is "when in doubt, use this one".
findings.fix: Write `robot extract --method MIREOT --input go.owl --lower-terms imports/go_terms.txt --output ...`. Correct the table to STAR = smallest (seed terms plus the axioms between them), BOT = seed terms plus superclasses (the default), TOP = seed terms plus subclasses (large).

verification.checked: ROBOT docs/extract.md says --term and --term-file seed the SLME methods (STAR, BOT, TOP), while MIREOT takes --upper-term(s), --lower-term(s) (a lower term is required) or --branch-from-term(s). STAR is "typically very small", BOT is "when in doubt, use this one", and TOP is "typically large". The scout's table (line 122) and its comment (line 144) call STAR the most complete. Line 101 only names the method, so the broken command is at lines 150-154.

findings.claim: The import recipe truncates `imports/go_terms.txt` with `echo ... >`, which wipes a curated term list. It then runs STAR and MIREOT to the same `--output imports/go_import.owl`, so the second command silently overwrites the first.
findings.evidence: Lines 141 and 148/154: the same output path for both methods, and `>` on an existing term file.
findings.fix: Show the two methods as alternatives with distinct outputs (`go_import.star.owl` and `go_import.mireot.owl`). Append with `>>` only after checking whether the file exists, or tell the agent to edit the term list rather than regenerate it.

verification.checked: Line 141 uses `>` on imports/go_terms.txt. Both extract commands in the same block write `--output imports/go_import.owl` (lines 148 and 154), so running the block as written overwrites the STAR module with the MIREOT one.

findings.claim: The triggers will fire on ordinary inventory-import work. Scout activates when the user mentions "reuse" or "import", and import is this app's core feature. Requirements fires on "requirements" and "create tests or acceptance criteria" (its description says "creating acceptance tests"). Conceptualizer fires on "model" and "hierarchy".
findings.evidence: inventory-import CLAUDE.md: the product is "the import of a file of items", and its tests and requirements are everyday words there.
findings.fix: Upstream: qualify every trigger with ontology context, for example "ontology reuse/owl:imports", "competency questions for an ontology" or "class hierarchy of an OWL/SKOS vocabulary". In each description, also say when the skill should not fire (app data import, software tests). Adapt: point the descriptions at the erp-ontology packet and the vocabulary module.

verification.checked: A skill is chosen from its frontmatter description; the body's "When to Activate" list is read only after the skill has loaded. Two of the three descriptions are already qualified for ontologies: scout says "existing ontologies to reuse or align with" and conceptualizer says "designing the structure of an ontology". The real risk is requirements, whose description ends "defining scope, or creating acceptance tests" with no qualifier, and that is the text shown in this session's skill list. The body lists ("reuse", "import", "model", "hierarchy") are unqualified, but they matter less.
verification.correctedFix: Qualify the requirements description ("acceptance tests for an ontology's competency questions") and add a do-not-use clause to it (app data import, software tests). For scout and conceptualizer, qualifying the body lists and adding a negative clause is optional hardening.

findings.claim: The "Always-Reuse Baseline" puts "FOAF or schema.org: people/organization basics" in scope by default, and the reuse tree recommends "Direct Import | owl:imports" above 80% coverage. That yields a second person/organization vocabulary beside gist:Person and gist:Organization, and a whole-ontology import where the decision is a short projected term list.
findings.evidence: DECISIONS.md #4: "the projection is a list of imported terms", with IOF and ISA-95 as alignments only. #2: the Turtle is generated from the TS module.
findings.fix: Adapt: the baseline becomes gist (projection), SKOS, dcterms and PROV-O as annotation and provenance. schema.org, FOAF, IOF and ISA-95 appear only as alignment rows. The strategy table maps any coverage level to either 'add terms to the gist projection list' or 'alignment row (ontology-mapper)'. No owl:imports or extracted OWL module is committed.

verification.checked: Scout lines 39-50 include "FOAF or schema.org: people/organization basics" by default, and line 99 maps coverage above 80% to Direct Import with owl:imports. DECISIONS #4 says the projection is a list of imported terms.

findings.claim: Search and quality criteria are OBO and biomedical: OLS, BioPortal, sqlite:obo, "OBO Dashboard score", "Uses RO relations?", and GO examples. LOV is named in the description but no LOV step is given. For an ERP or WMS domain, OLS returns SNOMED and ENVO hits (a live `search warehouse` returned SCTID and ENVO terms), and the relevant sources (gist, schema.org/GoodRelations, IOF core, ISA-95/B2MML, UN/CEFACT, GS1) are never mentioned.
findings.evidence: Live `runoak -i ols: search warehouse` returned SCTID:257727001 and ENVO:00003963. `lov:` is a valid oaklib adapter but the skill never uses it.
findings.fix: Upstream: make the registry list domain-dependent. Add a LOV step (`runoak -i lov: search` or the LOV API) and a non-OBO quality rubric (maintained releases, license, OWL 2 DL profile). Adapt: name gist, IOF core, ISA-95/B2MML, schema.org and GS1 as the candidates and drop the GO examples.

verification.checked: The description names LOV at line 5, but Steps 1 to 5 give no LOV command. The rubric relies on the OBO Dashboard and on RO relations, the examples are GO, and the workflow never mentions gist, schema.org/GoodRelations, IOF, ISA-95 or GS1. oaklib's resolver does have a `lov` scheme. I did not re-run the reviewer's live `search warehouse` result.

findings.claim: "Logical consistency | Required | `robot reason --reasoner ELK`". ELK covers only OWL 2 EL and ignores the axioms outside it (unions, universals, cardinality, inverse), so a candidate such as gist, which uses unionOf and cardinality, can pass while it is DL-inconsistent.
findings.evidence: axiom-patterns.md:179 already says "ELK does not support cardinality — use HermiT or Pellet". ROBOT's reason command supports `--reasoner hermit`, `whelk` and others.
findings.fix: Use `robot reason --reasoner HermiT` (or Whelk for large OWL RL) for candidates outside EL. Say that ELK is a fast EL-only check. Adapt: use whichever reasoner check:full adopts, which decision 6 says is still owed.

verification.checked: The claim is correct. Scout lines 86 and 211 use ELK for "Logical consistency", and axiom-patterns.md:179 itself says ELK does not support cardinality. Part of the fix is wrong: Whelk is an ELK-style EL reasoner (EL plus a few rule extensions), not an "OWL RL" reasoner, so it is just as incomplete for unions and cardinality.
verification.correctedFix: Use `robot reason --reasoner HermiT --input candidate.owl` for any candidate outside OWL 2 EL, and describe ELK and Whelk as fast checks that cover EL only. Adapt to the reasoner check:full adopts; DECISIONS #6 records that the choice of reasoner is still owed.

findings.claim: Anti-pattern #2 calls "roles as subclasses" (Person → Student) wrong and gives the fix `Person bearerOf some StudentRole`, which states that every Person bears a student role. Under OntoClean and UFO, which the auditor and foundational-analysis.md use, a role specializing a kind is correct; the error is an anti-rigid class subsuming a rigid one (ontoclean-rules.yaml:103). The conceptualizer therefore checks the auditor's ratified UFO roles against a rule that contradicts them.
findings.evidence: foundational-analysis.md:35: "Role | Anti-rigid, relationally dependent ... Classic bug: Role-as-kind". ontoclean-rules.yaml:103: "anti-rigid superclass with rigid subclass → BLOCK".
findings.fix: Rewrite #2 as "Role-as-kind: a role modelled as rigid or disjoint from its bearer kind, or a kind placed under a role". Allow `Student ⊑ Person` when Student is tagged anti-rigid. Fix the BFO axiom to `Student EquivalentTo Person and (bearerOf some StudentRole)`. The conceptualizer's item 2 then cites the OntoClean rule.

verification.checked: anti-patterns.md:42-64 and bfo-categories.md:106 do say what the reviewer quotes. The suggested fix `Person bearerOf some StudentRole` would make every Person bear a student role. foundational-analysis.md:35 defines Role-as-kind as modelling a role as a rigid class. Two citations are wrong. ontoclean-rules.yaml has only 22 lines; the rule "anti-rigid superclass with rigid subclass → BLOCK" is at line 7, not 103. The reviewer's evidence also cites foundational-analysis.md, which is not one of the three skills under review. The finding itself holds.

findings.claim: The conceptualizer's property template has an "Inverse" field and an "inverse-functional" characteristic, and naming-conventions requires inverse pairs ("hasPart / partOf"). The axiom catalogue it selects from maps "These two identifiers are the same individual" to owl:sameAs and "X is identified by P" to HasKey. Its HasKey note leaves out that the axiom entails owl:sameAs between named individuals that share key values, which makes it deduplication by sameAs.
findings.evidence: DECISIONS context (decision 3) says no owl:inverseOf and no owl:sameAs for deduplication. research/02 checks: "no owl:inverseOf or owl:sameAs". OWL 2 Direct Semantics: HasKey infers equality of named individuals.
findings.fix: Adapt: drop Inverse and inverse-functional from property-design. Name a single direction for each relation, and write the reverse in queries as a SPARQL `^p` path. Remove the sameAs and HasKey rows from the selection table, and model identity as the auditor's identity criterion with SHACL uniqueness over keys. Upstream: say that HasKey entails sameAs and applies only to named individuals.

verification.checked: The conceptualizer has an Inverse field (line 134) and an inverse-functional characteristic (line 133). naming-conventions.md:32-33 requires inverse pairs. axiom-patterns.md:370 and 372 map these cases to HasKey and sameAs. The reviewer overstates one point: the HasKey note (line 261) does say that individuals sharing key values "are considered identical", which is the sameAs entailment. What it leaves out is that this applies only to named individuals. The "no owl:inverseOf / owl:sameAs" rule comes from research/02 line 122, a planned `laws ontology-terms` rule, not from a numbered entry in DECISIONS.md.

findings.claim: The Missing Disjointness detection query uses `rdf:rest*/rdf:first` but declares only the rdfs and owl prefixes, so it fails to parse. Separately, the leaf-domain/range query (lines 300-321) flags every datatype range such as xsd:string as a 'leaf class', because it only filters with `isIRI`.
findings.evidence: Lines 107-109 declare rdfs and owl only, and line 123 uses rdf:. In the #10 query, xsd datatypes have no rdfs:subClassOf children.
findings.fix: Add `PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#>`. In #10 add `FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?narrowClass a rdfs:Datatype } FILTER(!STRSTARTS(STR(?narrowClass), STR(xsd:)))`, or restrict to `?narrowClass a owl:Class`.

verification.checked: The #4 query declares only the rdfs and owl prefixes (lines 108-109) but uses rdf:rest*/rdf:first at lines 123-124, so it fails to parse. In the #10 query, line 312 filters only with isIRI, so built-in xsd datatype ranges, which have no subclasses, are flagged. The suggested `?narrowClass a rdfs:Datatype` filter will not catch them either, because xsd built-ins are normally not declared as datatypes.
verification.correctedFix: Add `PREFIX rdf:` to #4. In #10, restrict the check to `?narrowClass a owl:Class`, or declare `PREFIX xsd:` and filter with `!STRSTARTS(STR(?narrowClass), STR(xsd:))`.

findings.claim: Anti-pattern #6 calls `Color → Red` wrong, then its fix `Color DisjointUnionOf Red, Blue, Green` is the same subclass hierarchy. bfo-categories says "Red as a subclass of Color" is a mistake because red is "a particular Quality value", while axiom-patterns #8 says "Each value is a class, not an individual". PATO and BFO do treat red as a subclass of color. The defect #6 should target is RedCar-style class proliferation.
findings.evidence: Three files give three incompatible rules for the same case.
findings.fix: Upstream: settle on one rule. Value partitions (value classes) are fine, and the anti-pattern is minting compound classes per value (RedCar). Fix the bfo-categories row to say "red is a determinate quality class under color". Adapt: code lists such as ItemRole are SKOS concept schemes in the vocabulary module (research/02), not OWL value partitions, so say when each applies.

verification.checked: anti-patterns.md:162-176 marks `Color → Red` as wrong, then gives the fix `Color DisjointUnionOf Red, Blue, Green`, which makes Red a subclass of Color. bfo-categories.md:108 calls Red a subclass of Color a mistake, while axiom-patterns.md:203-204 says "Each value is a class, not an individual." PATO makes red (PATO:0000322) a subclass of color.

findings.claim: There are four BFO and RO errors. (a) `RO:0000080 (has quality)` is wrong: RO:0000080 is 'quality of' and 'has quality' is RO:0000086. (b) Function is shown as a sibling of Disposition, but in BFO 2.0/2020 function is_a disposition. (c) Fiat Object Part is defined as "Part of an object, not self-connected", but it is a part demarcated by fiat boundaries and may be self-connected. (d) The Common Mistakes table marks "Organization as Object" wrong and prescribes Object Aggregate, while Known Ambiguities recommends Object as the default. Also, the GDC example calls "This PDF file" the material bearer although the tree lists a PDF document as a GDC.
findings.evidence: RO IDs in the OBO RO release. BFO-2020 OWL: BFO_0000034 subClassOf BFO_0000016. Lines 114 and 191 contradict each other within the file.
findings.fix: Correct the IDs and the tree, make the two organization rows agree (and point to BFO 2020 as a source), and change the GDC example to 'a file's content (GDC) concretized by a pattern (SDC) on a disk (material entity)'. Adapt: if a gist guide replaces this file, these errors drop out, but fix them upstream.

verification.checked: All four errors are at the cited lines. bfo-categories.md:127 says RO:0000080 is "has quality"; in RO, RO_0000080 is "quality of" and RO_0000086 is "has quality". Lines 53-59 show Function as a sibling of Disposition, but in BFO 2.0/2020 BFO_0000034 is a subclass of BFO_0000016. Line 35 defines Fiat Object Part as "not self-connected". Line 114 says Organization is an Object Aggregate while line 191 recommends Object. Line 157 calls the PDF file the material bearer while line 67 lists a PDF document as a GDC.

findings.claim: "regularity restrictions apply (R can appear at most once and only at the end of its own chain)". OWL 2 allows `R o R → R`, `R o S1..Sn → R` (R first) and `S1..Sn o R → R` (R last). Separately, `ReflexiveObjectProperty: partOf` (line 244) is functional-syntax naming presented as Manchester syntax.
findings.evidence: OWL 2 Structural Specification §11.2, regularity of the property hierarchy.
findings.fix: State the three permitted forms, and note that a property used in a chain becomes non-simple (it cannot then be used in cardinality, functional or disjoint axioms). Write the Manchester form `ObjectProperty: partOf  Characteristics: Reflexive`.

verification.checked: axiom-patterns.md:281-282 says "R can appear at most once and only at the end". OWL 2 Structural Specification §11.2 also allows R o R ⊑ R and R o S1..Sn ⊑ R. Line 244 uses the functional-syntax name ReflexiveObjectProperty in prose.

findings.claim: The anti-pattern section says "'What instruments exist?' cannot [fail]" and calls it vague. The skill's only formalized example, CQ-001, is "What instruments exist in the ontology?" with `expected_result: non_empty`. Step 7 covers only enumerative tests (non-empty) and constraint tests (zero rows). It gives no form for the boolean, relational, quantitative and temporal types it defines, and boolean CQs like "Is a piano a string instrument?" need an ASK under entailment, not plain SPARQL.
findings.evidence: Lines 121 and 256-259, and the Step 2 table at lines 87-94.
findings.fix: Replace CQ-001 with a CQ that can fail (with a fixture and a must-fail counterexample). Give the test shape for each CQ type: ASK for boolean, an expected-rows file for relational and quantitative. The plan is reasonable, but several commands are wrong in ways that cause harm. Three of the KGCL lines do not parse, and the OWLAPY imports fail on owlapy 1.6.7. For inventory-import the edit-the-Turtle model conflicts with decision 2, where Turtle is generated from the TypeScript vocabulary. unitSummary: _shared holds the ontology skill family's common references: the lifecycle, BFO decision trees, axiom patterns, anti-patterns, naming, tool tree, quality checklist, namespaces, OntoClean rules, the stage-authority matrix and eight record schemas. Its foundational discipline is sound: the six laws, the failure modes, and the rule that LLMs propose and humans ratify. The tool layer has real errors. Three of seven KGCL examples fail the KGCL parser. `robot verify` is used backwards for competency-question tests. Pellet is named as a ROBOT reasoner, and it is not one. Several SPARQL queries and ROBOT templates are broken. For inventory-import, the defaults (BFO, editing Turtle with ROBOT or KGCL, sameAs/HasKey/inverse pairs, pyshacl over the ontology) conflict with decisions 1 to 5.
keepAsIs: foundational-analysis.md: the six laws, the governing principle, the category cheat-sheet that treats software analogues as priors to test, and the full software-domain failure-mode table (enum-is-taxonomy, identifier-is-identity, domain/range-as-validation, vacuous green, OWA/CWA collapse) fit an ERP model built from code
stage-authority-matrix.yaml: the forbidden_autonomous_decisions list matches the rule that product decisions are Benjamin's, and the rule that only the human steward ratifies
schemas/denotation-hypothesis: the required null hypothesis with an observation-backed discriminator, and confidence marked use_for_acceptance: false
schemas/ratification: the per-proposal verbatim decision, and the proposal_sha256 staleness check

anti-patterns.md #10 (domain/range are inference rules; use SHACL to constrain), #13 false is-a from OO inheritance, #14 system blueprint instead of domain model, #15 technical perspective; all are directly relevant when terms come from TypeScript schemas
axiom-patterns.md: the closure-axiom note (a universal restriction alone is vacuous) and the SubClassOf-before-EquivalentClass default
methodology-backbone.md: the CQ through-line table and the phase entry/exit criteria
naming-conventions.md: genus-differentia definitions, one label per language, never reusing or changing a published IRI
tool-decision-tree.md: the oaklib known-limitations section (adapter inconsistency, pystow cache at ~/.data/oaklib); `runoak apply --changes-input` exists (checked with --help)

findings.claim: Three of the seven KGCL examples are not KGCL: "create class EX:0001 'New Term'", "move EX:0010 from EX:0001 to EX:0002" and "create definition 'A thing that...' for EX:0001".
findings.evidence: `uv run --with kgcl-schema` parse_statement gave UnexpectedCharacters for all three. These forms parse: `create node EX:0001 'New Term'` (NodeCreation), `add definition '...' to EX:0001` (NewTextDefinition), and `create edge EX:0001 rdfs:subClassOf EX:0002`. The grammar's `move` takes subject, predicate and object before `from`.
findings.fix: Replace them with `create node EX:0001 'new term'`, `add definition '...' to EX:0001`, and either `move EX:0010 rdfs:subClassOf EX:0001 from EX:0001 to EX:0002` or a delete edge plus a create edge. Add a note to dry-run every KGCL line with `runoak apply --dry-run` before applying it. Fix the copies in architect and curator.

There is no `create definition` rule: it is `add definition '<text>' to <id>`. `move` needs subject, predicate and object before `from`. architect SKILL.md:148 and 154 run the same broken forms through `uv run runoak ... apply`. I did not run a parser myself, because the task is read-only.

findings.claim: HasKey is described as "analogous to a database primary key" whose individuals "are considered identical". The selection guide sends "X is identified by P" to HasKey and "These two identifiers are the same individual" to owl:sameAs.

findings.fix: Upstream: add the caveat that HasKey covers named individuals only, infers sameAs, and does not validate; for uniqueness use SHACL or a database constraint. Inventory-import: delete pattern 14 and the two selection-guide rows, and say that identity of stored rows is decided by the import rules and Benjamin, never by OWL.

The table also gives `RO:0000080 (has quality)`.

The 'blinded' alternative seat can read work/foundational/, and every seat can write anywhere in the repo, including other seats' outputs. Blinding rests only on prompt wording. findings.claim: The canonical id formula is given only as Python `json.dumps(..., sort_keys, separators, ensure_ascii=False)`, but adapters must be Bun TypeScript. An agent's natural `pairs.sort()` sorts by the joined string in UTF-16 order, which differs from Python's sort of lists by code point for non-BMP or comma-bearing objects.

findings.fix: Add the exact JS form: `JSON.stringify([commit,path,start,end,pairs.toSorted(cmpCodePoint),id,version])`, with a code-point comparator.

findings.claim: The rule list leaves out two of OntoClean's core subsumption constraints. A property carrying anti-unity (~U) cannot subsume one carrying unity (+U), and a dependent property (+D) cannot subsume a non-dependent one (-D). Both meta-properties are recorded (IC `unity`, `dependence`), but no rule uses them.
findings.evidence: Guarino & Welty, 'An Overview of OntoClean' (2004), constraints on +O/+I/+R/+U/+D.
findings.fix: Add two REVIEW rules for unity and dependence along is-a edges.

verification.checked: ontoclean-rules.yaml has no unity or dependence edge rule. Guarino & Welty's OntoClean constraints include '~U cannot subsume +U' and '+D cannot subsume -D' (and '+U cannot subsume -U'). A further problem: the IC's ontoclean.unity is a free string, so no such rule could be made mechanical without a closed enum.
verification.correctedFix: Add the REVIEW rules, and make ontoclean.unity a closed enum (+U | -U | ~U | unresolved) so that the rules can be checked.
